This evaluation covered 11 eval scenarios (one skipped as not applicable: "unrelated-lambda-cold-start", since should_trigger was false), each run 3 times, all 63 iterations completing without failure.

**Trigger firing**: In every eval where it applied, the behavior under test fired 100% of the time for both variants — this dimension shows no difference and isn't informative here.

**Meeting expected output**: This is the most consistent and largest difference in the data. with_skill met the expected output in nearly all evals (typically 3/3 or 100%, with one eval at 2/3 and one at 2/3/67%), while without_skill met it much less often — 0/3 in six of the nine applicable evals, 1/3 in one, 2/3 in one, and only in the two "serverless" and "data-pipeline" evals did without_skill match with_skill at 3/3. Confidence behind these judgments was generally high to medium, so this is a reasonably solid signal, not a low-confidence artifact.

**Per-assertion pass rates**: with_skill scored very high across almost all evals (90–100%, with one eval at 100% exactly and most others 93-100%), while without_skill's assertion pass rates were markedly lower in most evals (ranging from 28% to 75%), except for "dr-start-named-resource-missing" where both variants hit 100%, and "dr-start-ecs-api" and "dr-start-k8s" where without_skill reached 38–67%. Looking at individual assertions rather than aggregates: several assertions passed for both variants consistently (e.g., "no create/modify/delete API call reported," "does not mention other workloads' resources," "does not state RPO/RTO as targets") — these are not discriminating and reflect behaviors both variants handle reliably. Other assertions, especially around structural requirements (six required section headings in order, roadmap grouping into quick wins/fixes/long-term, naming specific resources/replication gaps) consistently passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill across many evals — a recurring, specific pattern rather than a one-off. A few assertions were flaky (partial pass rates) for one or both variants, indicating some run-to-run variability in borderline checks.

**Runtime and cost**: without_skill was consistently and substantially faster and cheaper than with_skill across every eval — often by multiples (e.g., runtimes of ~1-4 minutes vs. with_skill's ~3-7 minutes, and costs roughly 1/3 to 1/2 of with_skill's). This is a clear, consistent pattern throughout.

**Quality comparisons (head-to-head pairs)**: Where pairwise quality comparisons were possible (several evals had 0 pairs evaluated/skipped, limiting what can be said), with_skill was favored more often than without_skill on accuracy, completeness, and mostly on actionability (though without_skill was favored on actionability in a couple of pairs). Confidence on these comparisons was generally medium to high. Many evals had all quality pairs skipped, so this dimension's coverage is partial and shouldn't be over-weighted.

**Output consistency (run-to-run stability)**: Where measured, with_skill ranged from "consistent" to "mostly_consistent" (one eval showed "inconsistent" for with_skill on one dimension). without_skill's consistency was often not measured (null) in several evals, and where measured, ranged from "mostly_consistent" to "consistent," similar to with_skill. Coverage for this dimension is incomplete for without_skill in particular, so conclusions here are limited.

**Overall pattern**: Across these DR-readiness-assessment evals, with_skill more reliably matched the expected output and passed structural/content assertions (particularly around required headings, roadmap structure, and specific resource-level findings), while without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper to run. This is a tradeoff between speed/cost and thoroughness/compliance with expected format and content, rather than a one-sided result — though the magnitude of the expected-output and assertion gaps is large and recurs across most evals, which is a notable and consistent pattern rather than noise. Some assertions and whole dimensions (quality pairs, consistency for without_skill) had limited or no data, so those specific aspects carry lower certainty.
